rationale: A wins because it protects the founder from the obvious killshot: no named utility and no FAA details, instead of turning those gaps into scenery. Its line "without a named utility it has no second life" is the kind of ugly truth that saves a pitch. B has a real regulatory angle, but it opens with "Autonomous drones start patrolling America's power grid without a pilot in sight," which sounds bigger than the facts and starts spending credibility before the reporter has even replied.
gaps_in_A: "A drone with no pilot is a shot at the inspection business built on pilots" overreaches. The update says no pilot; it does not say Skydio is displacing inspection contractors, pilots, jobs, or service contracts.
"The launch is the first hard evidence" is not in the update. Two years after the consumer exit is fair; claiming this is the first proof point needs history the prompt did not provide.

A treats FAA authorization mostly as proof support instead of giving the regulatory angle its own full shape. For scheduled no-pilot infrastructure flights, that may be the sharpest reporter question in the whole announcement.
gaps_in_B: "Autonomous drones start patrolling America's power grid without a pilot in sight" overstates the facts. A launch plus unnamed utility contracts is not proof that drones are already patrolling America's grid.
"wildfire-risk mitigation" is imported context. The update mentions power lines and substations, not wildfires, wildfire prevention, or grid-fire programs.

"Power-line and substation inspection is dangerous, manual, and expensive work utilities have wanted to automate for years" may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts. That is background a reporter would demand sourced, not a free decorating clause.
"None of these four angles has a fatal hole" is too soft. No named utility and no flight-authorization specifics can absolutely kill the operations and no-pilot angles.
